title: C2 Proficiency English Examination (CEFR / CPE Standard)
description: Extremely demanding CEFR C2 assessment of Reading and Listening comprehension for near-native candidates (Cambridge C2 Proficiency level). Four dense argumentative reading texts and four fast-paced listening parts test inference, writer attitude, implicit meaning, paraphrase and fine discrimination between near-synonymous options. 44 questions, approximately 95 minutes.

reading.instructions: Read the four passages carefully and answer all questions from r-q1 to r-q24. Many questions require you to infer the writer's purpose or attitude rather than locate a stated fact. For multiple-select questions, choose exactly the number of answers required; no partial credit is awarded. For fill-in-the-blank questions, write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS or a number, using words from the passage.

passages.title: The Tyranny of the Definitive Edition
passages.content:
Few phrases in publishing carry as much unexamined prestige as "the definitive edition". Printed on a dust jacket, it promises a text purged of corruption — a work restored to what its author truly meant. Yet textual scholars, who spend their careers among the manuscripts, proofs and marginalia from which such editions are assembled, tend to wince at the adjective. They know that a definitive edition is less a discovery than a decision, and that the decision conceals a contest between rival versions of the same work, each with a plausible claim to authority.

Consider the typical predicament. A novelist submits a typescript; her editor, a conscientious man with a taste for tidy syntax, alters perhaps two hundred sentences; a compositor, working from a barely legible carbon, introduces errors of his own; the author, reading proofs under deadline, accepts some changes, reverses others and overlooks the rest. Decades later, a scholar must determine which of the readings now on the page are the author's and which are the debris of the process. The orthodox answer, formulated in the mid-twentieth century, was that the editor should reconstruct the author's "final intentions", treating every intervening hand as an obstruction to be cleared away. The method had the attraction of coherence: a text, like a statue, was imagined to exist in its perfect form in the sculptor's mind, with everything that followed amounting to the chipping and cracking of transmission. Not every alteration along the way was an improvement, nor every one a corruption; many were simply different, and it is precisely the difference that the scholar is obliged to adjudicate.

The difficulty is that authors seldom behave as the model assumes. Many write collaboratively without admitting it, and some positively welcome the intrusions of editors, spouses and friends. Others revise compulsively, so that "final" becomes an arbitrary halting point, determined less by artistic conviction than by the printer's patience. The poet who emends the same stanza in four successive editions has not been progressing towards a single ideal; she has been inhabiting, in turn, four different poems. To canonise the last of them simply because it is last is to mistake chronology for authority.

A later generation of scholars, impatient with the cult of the solitary genius, proposed a different emphasis: the "social text". On this view, a book is the product of a network that includes publishers, printers, censors and readers, and any attempt to isolate the author's pure contribution is not merely impracticable but conceptually confused. The insight was liberating, and it rescued many neglected versions from oblivion. But it brought a hazard of its own. If every version is equally the outcome of a social process, on what grounds might an editor prefer one? Pressed to its limit, the position dissolves editing into cataloguing, and the scholar becomes a custodian of variants who declines to say which of them a reader ought to read — a stance that sits awkwardly with the reader's perfectly reasonable wish to read something.

It is here that the "definitive edition" reasserts its appeal, and here that the case against it needs to be made with most care. The objection is not that such editions are useless; they are indispensable. It is that the word "definitive" disguises a judgement as a fact. An edition that establishes its text from the earliest manuscript will give readers something startlingly different from one that follows the first printing, and different again from one that follows the version through which the work actually entered the culture. Each choice has a rationale; none is neutral. The honest edition is therefore the one that makes its choices visible, printing its apparatus of variants not as an appendix for specialists but as an integral part of what it offers. Readers seldom notice that a decision has been taken on their behalf, because the authority of an edition is performed in its introduction, its binding and its air of finality quite as much as in its text.

Digital publication makes this more feasible than ever. A reader can now move between versions of a poem at the click of a button, watching a line mutate across a century. Traditionalists fear that such abundance will bewilder the casual reader, who, they suppose, wants only a book. The fear underestimates readers, and it overestimates the stability of the object they have been reading all along. Anyone who has met a beloved novel in two paperback editions, and been startled to discover that a paragraph is missing from one, has already learned what textual scholars have always known: that a book is less an object than an event, one that recurs whenever someone decides what it shall be.

None of this licenses relativism. Some readings are demonstrably corrupt: a compositor's misreading that converts sense into nonsense deserves no democratic hearing. The task is to distinguish between errors, which can be corrected, and variants, which can only be chosen between — and to be candid about which is which. A scholar who confesses uncertainty is not abdicating authority but earning it. The reader, offered the text with its seams showing, is finally treated as a serious work has always assumed her to be: a participant in the making of its meaning rather than a consumer of its finish.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, the writer's point about the phrase 'the definitive edition' is that it

options.text: is a marketing device which scholars regard as vulgar
was coined by publishers to replace the notion of an author's final intentions
presents the outcome of a choice between rival versions as though it were a discovery
implies that no manuscript evidence for the work has survived

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that a definitive edition is 'less a discovery than a decision' which conceals a contest between rival versions. Nothing in the paragraph suggests the phrase is vulgar, newly coined, or tied to lost manuscripts.

questions.prompt: The writer argues that the 'final intentions' approach to editing is flawed in its internal logic.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the method 'had the attraction of coherence'. The writer's objection in paragraph 3 is empirical — authors seldom behave as the model assumes — not that the model is illogical.

questions.prompt: The writer mentions the poet who emends the same stanza in four successive editions in order to suggest that

options.text: a version's being the latest does not in itself give it greater authority
poets are less reliable guides to their own intentions than novelists are
each revision brings a work closer to the form its author envisaged
differences between editions are usually attributable to printers rather than authors

questions.explanation: The poet has been 'inhabiting four different poems', so canonising the last 'simply because it is last' is 'to mistake chronology for authority' (paragraph 3).

questions.prompt: Which TWO criticisms of the 'social text' approach does the writer make?

options.text: It has led scholars to neglect versions that were previously valued.
It undervalues the contribution that publishers and printers make to a book.
It leaves the editor without a principled basis for preferring one version to another.
It reduces the editor to a custodian of variants who will not advise readers.
It rests on evidence that has since been discredited.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'on what grounds might an editor prefer one?' (no principled basis for preference) and the scholar becomes 'a custodian of variants who declines to say which of them a reader ought to read'. The approach is said to have rescued neglected versions, so the claim that it led to neglect is the reverse of the text.

questions.prompt: Authors who revise compulsively often stop, the writer suggests, not out of artistic conviction but because a printer's ________ has run out. (ONE WORD)
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: the halting point is 'determined less by artistic conviction than by the printer's patience'.

questions.prompt: The writer believes that readers are better able to cope with competing versions of a text than traditionalists assume.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 6: 'The fear underestimates readers.'

passages.title: Pricing the Reef
passages.content:
For several decades, a dominant strategy in conservation has been to translate the natural world into the language of the balance sheet. Wetlands filter water, mangroves blunt storm surges, reefs shelter fisheries and draw tourists; each of these services, the argument runs, has a market equivalent, and once that equivalent is calculated, governments and investors can no longer pretend that protecting nature is a luxury. The appeal is obvious. A finance ministry that has remained deaf to appeals founded on beauty or obligation may prove rather more receptive to a spreadsheet. The strategy has produced real successes: some national accounts now record the depletion of forests and fisheries alongside the growth of output.

Yet the strategy has always carried a wager within it: that the sums will come out in nature's favour. Consider a hypothetical but entirely typical case, in which a developer proposes to drain an estuarine marsh for a container port. A rigorous valuation of the marsh's flood protection and its role as a nursery for fish might yield, say, forty million a year. The port, over the same period, promises sixty. Nothing in the method, after all, guarantees that the marsh will prove the more profitable of the two. By the logic of the ledger the marsh should lose, and those who sponsored the valuation have no principled ground on which to protest. They have conceded in advance that the matter is to be settled by arithmetic.

Defenders reply that this is precisely the point: honest accounting obliges developers to reckon with costs they would otherwise pass on to others, and the true worth of the marsh, properly measured, usually exceeds what a hasty calculation suggests. There is something in this; more than one destructive scheme has been abandoned once its hidden costs were quantified. But the reply is incomplete in two respects. First, it presumes that whatever matters can be assigned a figure, when the services most vital to a society's long-term survival — the stability of the climate, the resilience of a food web — are exactly those whose worth is least amenable to calculation, since nobody can say in advance what their loss would entail. Second, it overlooks what economists and psychologists call "crowding out": the tendency of a commercial vocabulary to displace the other reasons people have for acting.

The evidence for crowding out is suggestive rather than conclusive. In studies of communities asked whether they would accept an unwelcome facility, such as a waste repository, in their neighbourhood, an offer of compensation has sometimes lowered rather than raised the proportion willing to agree, apparently because payment recast a civic obligation as a commercial transaction. If a similar dynamic operates in conservation, then describing a river chiefly as a supplier of purification services worth so many millions may corrode the very sense of stewardship on which its protection ultimately depends. Citizens who have been taught to see the river as an asset can hardly be blamed for selling it when a better offer arrives.

There is, moreover, a problem of substitutability that the language of prices conceals. Once a service has a price, it invites comparison with whatever else might supply it more cheaply. If a marsh's flood protection is worth forty million a year, the logical question is whether a concrete sea wall could provide the same protection for thirty. The ecologist may reply that the marsh also nurtures fish, filters pollutants and shelters migrating birds, none of which a sea wall does; but each of these functions must then be priced in turn, and the argument has quietly moved onto ground where the sea wall's engineers are better equipped to fight.

A further difficulty is technical but decisive. Valuations of long-lived ecosystems depend on discount rates, which shrink the worth of future benefits in order to reflect the preference for present over later returns. At a rate of five per cent, a benefit arriving in a century is reduced to less than one per cent of its nominal worth. A reef that might sustain a fishery for hundreds of years therefore appears, on paper, scarcely more valuable than one that will be dead in a generation. Economists are well aware of the problem, and have proposed lower or declining rates for distant horizons; but the choice among these remedies is itself a value judgement, smuggled into a calculation that was supposed to be objective.

Nor is the alternative — a purely ethical case against destruction — free of difficulty. Appeals to the intrinsic worth of nature are notoriously unpersuasive in cabinet rooms, and tend to be weighed, by electorates, against the immediate claims of employment. Pragmatists therefore advocate a hybrid: use valuation defensively, to expose the concealed costs of damaging schemes, while refusing to treat it as the final arbiter. A figure may be deployed to embarrass a bad project, but never to authorise one. Whether that discipline can be sustained on the first occasion that the numbers fail to support the conservationist's case is, I suspect, the real test of the approach — and it is a test that has so far been avoided rather than passed.

questions.prompt: What does the writer mean by saying that the valuation strategy 'carries a wager within it' (paragraph 2)?

options.text: that investors will favour projects which offer ecological benefits
that conservation will prove cheaper to carry out than development
that governments will fund valuations in order to be seen to protect nature
that calculations of nature's worth will turn out to favour preservation

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines the wager directly: 'that the sums will come out in nature's favour'.

questions.prompt: In the writer's example, the estimated annual value of the marsh is greater than the annual benefit promised by the port.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the marsh might be valued at 'forty million a year' while the port 'promises sixty'.

questions.prompt: Which TWO weaknesses in the defenders' reply does the writer identify?

options.text: It exaggerates the extent to which developers conceal costs from the public.
It underplays the number of projects that have been halted by valuation.
It takes it for granted that whatever matters most can be given a figure.
It ignores the expense of carrying out valuations.
It neglects the way a commercial vocabulary can undermine other reasons for acting.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'First, it presumes that whatever matters can be assigned a figure'; 'Second, it overlooks ... crowding out'. The writer actually concedes that some schemes have been abandoned once their costs were quantified.

questions.prompt: At a discount rate of five per cent, a benefit due in a hundred years is reduced to less than ________ of its nominal worth.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5: 'a benefit arriving in a century is reduced to less than one per cent of its nominal worth'.

questions.prompt: The writer states that crowding out has been observed more frequently in wealthy societies than in poor ones.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 discusses evidence for crowding out but says nothing about differences between wealthy and poor societies.

questions.prompt: What does the writer identify as 'the real test' of the hybrid approach?

options.text: whether valuations can be made accurate enough to command public trust
whether conservationists will keep to their principle when the figures run against them
whether electorates will accept ethical arguments in preference to economic ones
whether discount rates can be set so as to favour long-lived ecosystems

questions.explanation: Paragraph 6: the test is whether the discipline of using figures only defensively 'can be sustained on the first occasion that the numbers fail to support the conservationist's case'.

passages.title: Do Words Shape Worlds?
passages.content:
Few ideas in the study of language have been so persistently misrepresented as the hypothesis that the structure of a language influences the thought of those who speak it. In its popular form — attributed, with little justification, to two American linguists of the early twentieth century — the notion is that speakers of different languages inhabit incommensurable mental worlds, so that a person raised in one tongue cannot in principle grasp what a person raised in another takes for granted. Stated so baldly, the claim is easily refuted: translators succeed daily, and any child discovers that a concept lacking a word can be introduced by means of a sentence.

With the strong version discarded, researchers over the last three decades have pursued something subtler: not whether language determines thought, but whether it nudges it, and under what conditions. The question has become empirical rather than philosophical. A language that obliges its speakers to indicate, in every statement, whether they witnessed an event or merely heard about it may cultivate a habit of attending to sources of evidence. Speakers of languages that describe location by compass bearing rather than by reference to the body — "the cup is south of the plate" — appear to maintain a more constant sense of orientation than those who say "left" and "right". Such findings are intriguing, and they have attracted precisely the sort of popular enthusiasm that makes cautious scholars uneasy. Experiments on colour are similar in spirit: speakers of languages that divide the spectrum differently have been found to differ, by small margins, in how quickly they tell apart shades that straddle a category boundary in their own language but not in another.

Their unease is justified, for the central methodological problem has proved stubborn. People who share a language typically share much else: a landscape, an economy, a set of customs, a schooling. If speakers of one language behave differently from speakers of another, the difference may stem from any of these, and the language may be a bystander. Or the causal arrow may point the other way: a language may simply record what its speakers already find worth distinguishing, in which case it reflects a preoccupation rather than creating one. The much-repeated assertion that the Inuit possess scores of words for snow has become, through sheer retelling, less a finding than a cautionary tale about how readily such stories are inflated. And even where a community does maintain an elaborate vocabulary for some feature of its surroundings, that demonstrates little beyond expertise, which every specialist acquires.

Researchers have therefore turned to designs that can isolate the contribution of language itself. In a typical verbal-interference experiment, participants perform a task — sorting colours, say, or judging whether two arrangements of objects match — while simultaneously repeating a string of digits aloud, which occupies the verbal resources they would otherwise use to help them. If differences between speakers of different languages shrink or vanish under such interference, the likeliest explanation is that language was actively involved in producing them; if the differences persist, the culprit is probably something other than words. Even so, such designs are only as good as the tasks chosen, and a task that is easy to administer is not always one that language has any reason to touch. Results have been mixed, which is to say that the effects are neither universal nor imaginary.

A second line of enquiry holds that linguistic influence is strongest not in silent reflection but in what has been termed "thinking for speaking": the mental habits we adopt as we prepare to put something into words. A speaker of a language that demands a choice between formal and familiar address must, before opening her mouth, form a judgement about her relationship to the listener; a speaker of a language without that requirement need not. The habit might leave no trace when she is sitting quietly, but it is exercised dozens of times each day, and on this account that exercise is where language leaves its mark.

Universalists remain unpersuaded, and their objection deserves a fair hearing: even where an effect exists, it may amount to a difference of milliseconds in reaction time, of interest to a laboratory but of little consequence to a life. The tasks used to detect such effects are, moreover, often artificial, and it is far from obvious that behaviour in them predicts behaviour in the street, the market or the family. Relativists reply that small effects, exercised daily across a lifetime, may accumulate. The reply is plausible, but plausibility is not demonstration, and no study has yet shown that the cumulative consequences are anything other than modest.

The most suggestive evidence, to my mind, comes from bilingual people. When the same individuals are tested in one language and then in another, their responses are sometimes found to shift in the direction favoured by the language of the task. If so, the influence of language on thought looks less like a fixed lens through which a person sees the world than like a tool that can be picked up and put down — something a speaker uses, rather than something that uses her. That conclusion is less dramatic than the popular version, but it has the merit of being more likely to be true.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about the popular form of the hypothesis (paragraph 1)?

options.text: It was carefully qualified by the linguists who first proposed it.
It has been confirmed in its essentials by recent experiments.
It is widely held by contemporary linguists, who nevertheless deny it in public.
It is contradicted by everyday experience of translation, and its attribution is doubtful.

questions.explanation: The notion is attributed 'with little justification' to two linguists and is 'easily refuted: translators succeed daily'.

questions.prompt: The writer states that researchers have given up asking whether language influences thought.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: researchers now ask 'whether it nudges it, and under what conditions' — the question has become empirical, not abandoned.

questions.prompt: Some researchers argue that language leaves its mark chiefly in a process termed '________'. (THREE WORDS)
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5: influence is strongest in what has been termed 'thinking for speaking'.

questions.prompt: Which TWO alternative explanations for behavioural differences between speakers of different languages does the writer raise?

options.text: A language may merely record distinctions that its speakers already consider important.
Experimenters may unconsciously favour speakers of their own language.
Translators may have introduced inaccuracies into the data.
Speakers of different languages may differ in how well they understand the instructions.
A shared way of life may be responsible for both the language and the behaviour.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: people who share a language share much else, so 'the language may be a bystander'; alternatively 'a language may simply record what its speakers already find worth distinguishing'.

questions.prompt: What is the logic of the verbal-interference experiments described in paragraph 4?

options.text: If differences remain when verbal resources are occupied, language can play no part in thought.
If differences disappear when verbal resources are occupied, language was probably contributing to them.
If differences persist, the participants' vocabulary must have been too limited.
If differences disappear, the original task must have been badly designed.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: if differences 'shrink or vanish under such interference, the likeliest explanation is that language was actively involved in producing them'.

questions.prompt: The writer thinks that evidence from bilingual people suggests that the influence of language on thought is flexible rather than fixed.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 7: the influence looks 'less like a fixed lens ... than like a tool that can be picked up and put down'.

passages.title: What the Foreman Knew
passages.content:
When a manufacturer of optical glass, whose lenses had been prized for the better part of a century, moved production from its Victorian works to a purpose-built plant in the 1970s, the transfer was meticulously planned. Every specification was copied; every recipe, down to the grams of each ingredient and the temperature at each stage, was transcribed, checked and filed. Yet for nearly a decade the new plant's output was inferior to the old, marred by faint striations that no instrument could trace to any departure from the documented procedure. The cause emerged only gradually. The old works' foreman, who had retired after thirty-eight years at the furnaces, had been able to tell when a melt was ready by the colour of its glow and the sound the stirring rod made as it passed through the viscous mass. No one had thought to record this, because no one, least of all the foreman, regarded it as knowledge. It was simply what he did.

The episode illustrates what the philosopher Michael Polanyi meant when he observed that we can know more than we can tell. Much of what skilled practitioners know is not stored as propositions that can be recited, but embedded in perception and habit: the surgeon's feel for tissue, the chef's judgement of a sauce, the pilot's sense that something is not quite right. The pianist cannot explain how she shapes a phrase, and the cyclist cannot say how she keeps her balance; asked to try, each will usually describe something other than what she actually does. Such knowledge is called tacit, and its defining feature is that its possessor can demonstrate it far more readily than describe it.

The attempt to capture tacit knowledge in explicit form has a long and chastening history. In the 1980s, enthusiasm for so-called expert systems led teams of "knowledge engineers" to interview specialists in the hope of extracting the rules by which they worked and encoding them in software. The specialists were not being obstructive. They simply found that, when pressed for the rules, they produced generalisations that they promptly qualified, and then exceptions to the qualifications; the real basis of their judgement kept slipping away. Paradoxically, the most accomplished specialists often proved the least able to explain themselves. The resulting systems performed adequately on routine cases and failed on exactly those in which expertise matters most.

It might be supposed that the remedy is ever more thorough documentation. The truth is more awkward. Written procedures succeed best where they confine themselves to what can honestly be stated: the aviation checklist, for example, works because it covers a small number of steps whose omission would be catastrophic and whose performance requires no judgement. Where procedures stretch beyond that limit, they can corrode the skill they were meant to preserve. Workers who follow a protocol to the letter may cease to notice what it was designed to detect, and newcomers trained chiefly from manuals learn what to do without grasping why — a deficiency that becomes visible only on the day the manual proves inadequate.

Tacit knowledge is therefore transmitted, where it is transmitted at all, by older means. The apprentice does not so much receive instruction as absorb it, by working alongside someone more skilled, imitating, being corrected, and gradually acquiring a sense of what counts as good work that no one could have specified at the outset. Scholars of learning have observed that this process depends less on explicit teaching than on proximity: the novice learns by being allowed to participate, in a modest way, in the real activity of the workshop, and the community's standards seep into her judgement. The medieval guilds understood this well, which is why a journeyman's years of travel and subordination mattered more to them than any written treatise.

Modern organisations, unfortunately, are poorly designed to sustain such transmission. Restructuring thins out the middle ranks, outsourcing disperses the practitioners, and long overlaps between retiring staff and their successors are regarded as an indulgence. When the veterans leave, firms often commission "exit interviews" in a bid to retain what they know. The results are predictably disappointing. An interview elicits what can be said; and so the organisation congratulates itself on having captured its institutional memory when it has captured only the articulate surface of it. Even where organisations grasp the danger, the incentives point the wrong way: the cost of an unrecorded skill is invisible until the day it is needed, whereas the cost of a prolonged overlap appears in every quarter's accounts.

There is a final irony. Contemporary machine-learning systems, trained on vast quantities of examples rather than programmed with rules, appear to acquire a kind of know-how that their own designers cannot fully articulate. The problem of tacit knowledge has not been solved; it has migrated. Where once a veteran could not say how he recognised a flawed melt, we now possess systems that recognise patterns whose basis nobody — neither engineer nor machine — can state. We have, in short, built things that know more than they can tell, and we have yet to decide how much trust that deserves.

questions.prompt: Why did the new plant produce inferior glass for so long?

options.text: A skill which the foreman exercised had never been recorded because it was not recognised as knowledge.
The recipes had been transcribed inaccurately during the move.
The new furnaces could not reach the temperatures the old ones had achieved.
The workers at the new plant were unwilling to follow the documented procedure.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: every recipe was transcribed and checked, but the foreman's ability to judge a melt by its glow and sound went unrecorded because 'no one ... regarded it as knowledge'.

questions.prompt: The workers at the new plant were paid less than their counterparts at the old works.
questions.explanation: The passage says nothing about the wages of the workers at either site.

questions.prompt: The foreman had worked at the furnaces for ________ years before he retired. (ONE NUMBER)
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the foreman 'had retired after thirty-eight years at the furnaces'.

questions.prompt: Which TWO consequences of over-reliance on written procedures does the writer mention?

options.text: Workers may stop noticing the things that a procedure was designed to detect.
Experienced staff may resign in protest at being so closely supervised.
Procedures may become obsolete faster than they can be revised.
Firms may underestimate the cost of training.
Newcomers may learn what to do without understanding why.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: workers 'may cease to notice what it was designed to detect', and newcomers 'learn what to do without grasping why'.

questions.prompt: What does the writer imply about exit interviews?

options.text: They fail because retiring employees are reluctant to share what they know.
They would succeed if they were conducted by experienced knowledge engineers.
They tend to capture only that part of an employee's knowledge which can be put into words.
They are valuable chiefly as a supplement to apprenticeship.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 6: 'An interview elicits what can be said', so the firm has captured 'only the articulate surface' of its institutional memory.

questions.prompt: What irony does the writer see in contemporary machine-learning systems?

options.text: They have made the tacit knowledge of human experts easy to codify.
They reproduce the old problem in a new form, since their designers cannot fully explain their know-how.
They perform worse than the expert systems of the 1980s on rare cases.
They depend on a form of apprenticeship supervised by veterans.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 7: 'The problem of tacit knowledge has not been solved; it has migrated' — we have 'built things that know more than they can tell'.

parts.title: Restoring a Lost Silent Film

audioConfig.overallStyle: soundproof broadcast studio, close-mic vocal warmth, dry acoustics, intimate clarity; brisk native radio pace with quick turn-taking and dry humour

speakers.name: Helen
speakers.style: polished radio presenter, curious, quick to follow up

speakers.name: Marcus
speakers.style: warm, wry, fluent expert who thinks aloud

parts.transcript:
Helen: Welcome back to Archive Hour. My guest this morning is Marcus Ellery, who leads the film conservation unit at the Calder Institute. Marcus, I gather you've spent the better part of this year on a single film.
Marcus: A single film, yes, though it arrived in forty-one separate fragments. It's a comedy from nineteen twenty-six, long presumed lost, and it turned up in the attic of a former cinema in a small Welsh town. <chuckle> Which is, I'm afraid, where most of these discoveries happen. Attics, cellars, the occasional garden shed.
Helen: And how did you know what you'd actually found?
Marcus: Partly luck. One fragment included a title card with the producer's logo, and the cinema's old ledger was in the same attic, recording a booking of that title in nineteen twenty-seven. Archives are as much about paper as about film, you see — the paperwork is how you prove what the film is.
Helen: And I imagine the condition of the material wasn't ideal.
Marcus: Well, it was worse than that, though not in the way people assume. Everyone fears fire, because early film stock was made of nitrate, and nitrate is notoriously flammable. But fire, honestly, is the lesser problem — we have vaults designed for exactly that. What really worried us was the chemistry of decay. Nitrate degrades in stages: first the image fades and turns brownish, then the surface becomes sticky, then it softens into a kind of froth, and finally it crumbles to powder. Ours was somewhere around the second stage — sticky and, in places, fused into solid blocks.
Helen: Fused? So you can't simply unroll it.
Marcus: Absolutely not. If you tried, you'd tear the image away from its base. So we spent the first three months simply separating layers, in humidity chambers, a few frames a day. I'd originally estimated six weeks. <short pause> That was optimistic.
Helen: |I can imagine| Now, I understand you resisted pressure to use digital tools to repair the damaged frames.
Marcus: I did, and this is where it becomes, I think, philosophically interesting. Modern software can fill in a scratch, remove mould, even invent missing detail. The temptation is considerable — distributors would love a pristine copy. But the first principle of our profession is that anything we do must be reversible and transparent. So we digitise the film exactly as it is, damage and all, and any enhancement is applied only to a separate working copy and documented in full, so that a future conservator can see precisely what was done.
Helen: But isn't there a danger that audiences simply won't tolerate the flicker and the scratches?
Marcus: I used to think so. Then we screened two versions for a general audience — a hundred or so people, half of them seeing the untouched version and half a cleaned-up one — and afterwards asked which they preferred. I fully expected the clean one to win by a mile. In fact the split was almost even, and several people who'd watched the damaged version said the scratches made it feel — their word — "authentic". I'm not sure I'd go quite that far, but it did make me considerably less anxious about leaving the damage visible.
Helen: |Mm| And there's the old assumption that early films look comical because they're projected too fast.
Marcus: It's one of the most persistent myths in the field. Silent films were never shot at a standard rate. Cameras were hand-cranked, and operators varied the speed for effect, so there's no single correct projection speed. The twenty-four frames a second that we take for granted came later, with sound. For this film, we found the cinema's projection notes — the projectionist had pencilled "slow for love scene" beside one reel number. <laugh> So we settled on eighteen frames a second for most of it, rising to twenty for the chase.
Helen: Marvellous. And the music? Silent films were never really silent.
Marcus: Never. A cue sheet survived, folded inside one of the film cans, listing the tunes and when they were played. But we can't recover the actual performance, so we've commissioned a new score. I'll be frank: some colleagues think it would be more honest to show the film in silence. I disagree. A silent screening would be tidy, but historically false.
Helen: When will the public be able to see it?
Marcus: A premiere in March, at the Calder, followed by a national tour. And one thing we've decided, which isn't conventional: the final credits will list everyone who worked on the restoration — conservators, technicians, volunteers, everybody. After a year of this, frankly, I think they've earned it.
Helen: Marcus Ellery, thank you.
Marcus: Thank you.

parts.title: Why Experts Forecast Badly

audioConfig.overallStyle: large university lecture theatre, subtle natural hall echo, formal educational projection, dry wit, rapid native lecture delivery with deliberate rhetorical pauses

parts.transcript:
Lecturer: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to tackle a question that ought to embarrass a great many professionals: why is it that experts, who know so much, so often predict the future so badly?
Lecturer: Let me begin with a tournament. In the mid-nineteen-eighties, a researcher recruited a little under three hundred professional commentators — academics, government advisers, journalists, people paid, quite literally, for their opinions — and over the following twenty years collected something like twenty-eight thousand of their forecasts about political and economic events. <short pause> Then he waited, and scored them.
Lecturer: Now, you may have heard the headline: that the experts did no better than a dart-throwing chimpanzee. That is a slight exaggeration. They did somewhat better than random guessing. But they did worse than a very simple rule — namely, predicting that whatever was happening now would simply carry on. So: better than a chimpanzee, worse than a spreadsheet. <chuckle>
Lecturer: What interested the researcher more was the pattern within the results. He divided his experts, borrowing a phrase from an old essay, into hedgehogs and foxes. The hedgehogs knew one big thing — they had a single grand theory, and they applied it to everything. The foxes knew many small things; they drew on lots of sources, and they were constantly willing to revise. And the foxes forecast considerably better. Which is surprising, because the hedgehogs were the ones who sounded most impressive. And here's the detail I find most damning: the more famous the expert, the worse the forecasts. Media prominence correlated negatively with accuracy. <short pause> Think about that the next time a television pundit tells you what will happen next year.
Lecturer: So why does this happen? I'd like to propose three explanations, and I want you to note that "they don't know enough" is not among them. Subject knowledge, beyond a fairly modest threshold, turned out to add almost nothing. The problem lies elsewhere.
Lecturer: First: vagueness. Most forecasts are made in language so elastic that they can never be proved wrong. "There's a significant risk of instability." What counts as significant? Over what period? If instability occurs, the forecaster was right; if it doesn't, well, there was only ever a risk. A forecast that can't fail can't teach anybody anything.
Lecturer: Second: memory. We are remarkably poor at recalling what we previously believed. Once an outcome is known, people routinely misremember their earlier predictions as having been closer to the truth than they really were — hindsight bias, as it's called. So even when forecasts are specific, the forecaster often edits the record without noticing.
Lecturer: Third: incentives. A commentator is rewarded for being bold, vivid and memorable, not for being well calibrated. If you say there's a sixty per cent chance of recession, nobody remembers; if you declare that catastrophe is certain and you happen to be right once, you're a prophet for a decade. The market for opinion pays for confidence, and confidence is precisely what the evidence says we should distrust.
Lecturer: Now, what's the remedy? Later research — and here I'm thinking of a series of forecasting tournaments run over the last fifteen years or so — identified a small group of what were called "superforecasters", people whose accuracy was consistently high. They were not, for the most part, specialists. What they had in common was a method. They put numbers on everything — not "likely", but sixty-five per cent. They broke large questions into small ones. They updated in small increments as evidence came in, neither clinging to their first estimate nor lurching wildly. And they kept score, using a measure — the Brier /ˈbraɪər/ score, if you want to look it up — which penalises confident mistakes more heavily than cautious ones.
Lecturer: Is assigning probabilities a cure-all? Of course not. Numbers can create an illusion of precision; a figure like sixty-five per cent conveys a rigour that the underlying judgement may not possess. But I'd argue that's the lesser evil. A probability, even a flawed one, can be checked, and so it can be improved. A vague phrase can only be defended.
Lecturer: One last thought. The deepest lesson isn't, I think, about forecasting at all. It's about the relationship between confidence and knowledge. We instinctively treat a confident voice as an informed one. The evidence suggests the reverse is closer to the truth. For next week, then, I'd like you to read the two papers on the course page and make a single forecast of your own — with a probability attached — about an event that will have resolved by the end of term. We'll score them together. <short pause> Thank you.

parts.title: A Tutorial on Rewilding and Baselines

audioConfig.overallStyle: quiet university office, conversational proximity, natural speech dynamics, informal academic register with hesitations and tentative agreement

parts.transcript:
Hartley: Come in, Priya, and shut the door behind you. I've read your draft chapter twice, which I should say is a compliment.
Priya: <chuckle> I'll take it as one.
Hartley: Good. Overall, it's bolder than I expected. You're arguing that rewilding projects should abandon historical baselines altogether — no more "restore the landscape to how it was in sixteen hundred" — and judge success instead by ecological function. I admire the ambition. But let me play devil's advocate for a moment.
Priya: Please do. I'd rather hear it from you than from the examiners.
Hartley: My worry is that "function" is doing a great deal of unexamined work. If the only criterion is a functioning ecosystem, then any functioning ecosystem will do — including one dominated by introduced species. A baseline, however flawed, at least tells you what you're aiming at.
Priya: That's the objection I fear most, actually. But I think the baseline is a false comfort. In my case study — the Fenmoor project — the target year was set at seventeen hundred, and the reason was simply that it's when the first reliable survey was made. Not because the landscape was in any way pristine. By then it had already been shaped by centuries of grazing and drainage.
Hartley: Fair enough. So the baseline is arbitrary. But arbitrary isn't the same as useless. Here's a suggestion: don't discard the baseline — demote it. Treat it as a reference point rather than a target.
Priya: Hmm. A reference rather than a target. I hadn't thought of it quite like that. That might actually pre-empt the objection, mightn't it? Because I could still use it as a yardstick without being bound by it.
Hartley: |Exactly| Now, structure. Your second section spends nearly three thousand words on the history of the idea of wilderness, and only eight hundred on your own case study. The proportions are the wrong way round.
Priya: I wondered about that. It's just that I found the history so fascinating I couldn't bring myself to cut it.
Hartley: I understand, but I'm afraid the examiners won't be rewarding fascination. Cut the history to about a thousand words and give the space to the case study. In particular, the beaver data. It's your most original material, and at present it's buried in a footnote.
Priya: The beaver data — yes. The dams seemed to reduce downstream flooding by something like twenty per cent, but the sample was tiny. A single catchment, two winters. I didn't feel it could bear much weight.
Hartley: Then say so. Report it, with the caveat, up front. Honest caution reads as strength, not weakness; a reader who sees you flagging the limits of your own evidence will trust the rest of it more.
Priya: That's a good point. I've been treating the small sample as something to apologise for, rather than something to be upfront about.
Hartley: Quite. And a smaller thing: your interviews with the local farmers. You've got twelve, and the tone of your discussion is rather defensive, as if their hostility to the project were a problem for your argument.
Priya: Well, it is a bit awkward, isn't it? They're mostly against it.
Hartley: But it's data, Priya. It's arguably the most interesting data you have. Why are they against it? Their reasons tell you where the "function" argument runs into things it hasn't accounted for — livelihoods, a sense of place. Don't apologise for the hostility; analyse it.
Priya: Right. So the farmers' objections become part of the argument rather than a footnote to it. To be honest, I did wonder whether the hostility was just a vocal minority.
Hartley: Then find out. Work out how many of the twelve actually object, and on what grounds — I'd guess you'll find three or four distinct reasons — and say so plainly. And while you're at it, watch the word "restoration". It smuggles the baseline straight back in, and you use it a dozen times in your first section.
Priya: A dozen? <chuckle> I'll do a search and replace tonight.
Hartley: Precisely. If you can do that, the chapter's much stronger. As for the conclusion, I'll hold my fire until I've seen the rest. Can I have a revised version by the end of the month?
Priya: That's about three weeks. I think so — if I stop rereading the wilderness material. <laugh>
Hartley: <chuckle> Do. And let's meet on the twelfth to go through it. Same time?
Priya: The twelfth — fine. Thank you, Dr Hartley.

parts.title: The Quiet Streets Experiment

audioConfig.overallStyle: broadcast news studio, crisp authoritative delivery, dry acoustics, dense information at native bulletin pace

parts.transcript:
[Short news jingle]
Newsreader: Good evening. Our main report tonight concerns something that, for most of us, barely registers until it disappears: quiet. The city of Marlbury this week published first-year results from its Quiet Streets scheme, the most ambitious attempt by any British city to treat noise as a public health problem rather than a mere nuisance.
Newsreader: Noise has long been the poor relation of urban policy. Air pollution attracts targets, legislation and campaigners; noise attracts, at best, a sigh. Yet the council's own survey found that it ranked second only to potholes among residents' complaints, and health researchers have for years linked chronic night-time noise to disturbed sleep and raised stress.
Newsreader: The pilot covers twenty-three streets in the city's eastern districts, home to some nineteen thousand people. Three measures were introduced. First, a speed limit of twenty miles an hour throughout the zone. Second, restrictions on night-time deliveries, with lorries barred from loading between eleven at night and six in the morning. And third, the resurfacing of the busiest roads with a low-noise asphalt designed to dampen the sound of tyres. Most comparable schemes elsewhere have relied on a single measure, usually a lower speed limit; Marlbury's planners say it is the combination that sets theirs apart. Before the scheme, the busiest street in the zone averaged just over sixty decibels at night, roughly the level of ordinary conversation. The council has spent around four million pounds on the pilot, most of it on the resurfacing.
Newsreader: The headline result is a fall in average night-time noise of about three decibels. Now, three decibels sounds trivial, and in perceptual terms it nearly is: to most listeners, a change of that size is barely noticeable. But the decibel scale is logarithmic, which means that a drop of three represents a halving of the sound energy reaching the ear. The council's consultants argue that this is why the health findings are more encouraging than the raw figure suggests. In the residents' survey, the proportion reporting that they were regularly woken at night fell from thirty-one per cent to nineteen per cent.
Newsreader: The scheme has, however, attracted opposition. The Marlbury Night Economy Forum, which represents the owners of bars and clubs, objects to a proposal to extend the zone into the city centre, arguing that tighter controls on late-night traffic would deter customers and cost jobs. The Regional Haulage Association, meanwhile, says the delivery ban has simply pushed lorries onto the roads in the early evening, adding congestion and cost for the firms concerned. Support, by contrast, has come from several quarters: residents' associations, cycling campaigners, and the local hospital trust, which reports fewer complaints from patients on wards overlooking the main road.
Newsreader: The council has also conceded a drawback. The low-noise asphalt works well when new, but its benefit fades as the surface wears, and engineers expect it will have to be replaced after about eight years, roughly half the life of conventional asphalt. Whether that expense is justified will, the council says, depend on whether the gains in sleep prove durable.
Newsreader: Which raises the question of how the scheme's success ought to be judged. The deputy leader of the council, Rosalind Achebe /əˈtʃeɪbeɪ/, was clear on this point. "We can measure decibels perfectly well," she said, "but what we are really trying to measure is whether people sleep. A street that is quieter on paper, and no better to live on, is not a success." The council will therefore combine readings from its noise monitors with a repeat of the residents' survey on sleep and wellbeing, and Ms Achebe has insisted that the two carry equal weight.
Newsreader: Further afield, other councils are watching closely. Two neighbouring authorities have already asked to see the data, though both stress that they are not yet committed to anything similar. A public consultation opens next month, and the council has promised to publish both the noise readings and the survey results in full. A vote on whether to extend the scheme is expected in the spring. Until then, the residents of those twenty-three streets will, perhaps, be sleeping a little better — and the rest of us may be listening a little more carefully.
